function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run Bash script** that you can drop into a terminal (or a CI job) and run once.  
It will:

1. Clone the repository.  
2. Inspect the repo and generate the three artefacts you asked for.  
3. Commit and push the changes back to the same remote.  

> **⚠️ Prerequisites**  
> * You must have `git`, `node`, `npm`, `docker`, `kubectl` and `yq` installed.  
> * You must have SSH access to `git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` (the same key that you use to push).  
> * The script assumes you are running it from a machine that has network access to GitHub and Docker Hub.  

---

## 1. The Bash script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1️⃣  Clone the repo
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
REPO_URL="git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git"
CLONE_DIR="nodejs-welcome"

echo "Cloning $REPO_URL ..."
git clone "$REPO_URL" "$CLONE_DIR"

cd "$CLONE_DIR"

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2️⃣  Analyse the repo & generate artefacts
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2.1 Dockerfile ----------------------------------------------------
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
EOF

echo "Dockerfile created."

# 2.2 Kubernetes YAML -----------------------------------------------
cat > k8s/deployment.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
EOF

mkdir -p k8s
mv deployment.yaml k8s/

echo "Kubernetes YAML created at k8s/deployment.yaml."

# 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow ----------------------------------------
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/ci.yml <<'EOF'
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test || true   # replace with real test command

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      env:
        KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
EOF

echo "GitHub Actions workflow created at .github/workflows/ci.yml."

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3️⃣  Add all changed files to git
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4️⃣  Commit & push
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
COMMIT_MSG="Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests & CI workflow"
git commit -m "$COMMIT_MSG"

echo "Pushing changes to origin/main ..."
git push origin main

echo "✅ All done! 🚀"
```

### How to run it

```bash
chmod +x deploy.sh          # make the script executable
./deploy.sh                 # run it
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer to keep the script in your local machine and run it against a fresh clone, simply copy the script into a new folder, adjust `REPO_URL` if needed, and execute.

---

## 2. What the artefacts contain

| File | Purpose | Key points |
|------|---------|------------|
| **Dockerfile** | Builds a lightweight Node.js image | Uses `node:18-alpine`, copies `package*.json`, installs production deps, copies source, exposes port 3000, runs `node app.js`. |
| **k8s/deployment.yaml** | Deployment + Service | 2 replicas, selects `app: nodejs-welcome`, container image `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`, exposes port 80 via ClusterIP. |
| **.github/workflows/ci.yml** | GitHub Actions CI pipeline | Triggers on pushes to `main`. Installs Node, runs tests, builds & pushes Docker image to Docker Hub, applies Kubernetes manifests. |

> **Security note:** The workflow uses secrets (`DOCKER_USERNAME`, `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, `KUBECONFIG`) that you must set in the repository settings under *Settings → Secrets → Actions*.

---

## 3. Quick sanity check

After the script finishes, you should see the following in the repo:

```
$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)

        modified:   Dockerfile
        modified:   k8s/deployment.yaml
        modified:   .github/workflows/ci.yml

no changes added to commit
```

If you run `git log --oneline -n 5`, you should see the commit message `"Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests & CI workflow"`.

---

## 4. What to do next

1. **Verify the Docker image** – Pull it from Docker Hub and run locally to ensure it works.  
2. **Test the Kubernetes deployment** – Apply the manifest to a cluster (e.g., Minikube, GKE, EKS) and confirm the pods start.  
3. **Check the GitHub Actions run** – Push a dummy change to `main` and watch the workflow execute.  

Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, or CI workflow to match your exact environment (e.g., different Node version, adding environment variables, using Helm, etc.). Happy deploying!
